prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

“Stephen Smith, University of Iowa sophomore, burned what he said was his draft card” and Norman Morrison, Quaker, of Baltimore Maryland, burned what he said was himself. You, Robert McNamara, burned what you said was a concentration of the Enemy Aggressor. No news medium troubled to put it in quotes. And Norman Morrison, Quaker, of Baltimore Maryland, burned what he said was himself. He said it with simple materials such as would be found in your kitchen. In your office you were informed. Reporters got cracking frantically on the mental disturbance angle. So far nothing turns up. Norman Morrison, Quaker, of Baltimore Maryland, burned, and while burning, screamed. No tip-off. No release. Nothing to quote, to manage to put in quotes. Pity the unaccustomed hesitance of the newspaper editorialists. Pity the press photographers, not called. Norman Morrison, Quaker, of Baltimore Maryland, burned and was burned and said all that there is to say in that language. Twice what is said in yours. It is a strange sect, Mr. McNamara, under advice to try the whole of a thought in silence, and to oneself.

outputs.L1:
“Stephen Smith, a University of Iowa sophomore, burned what he said was his draft card,” and Norman Morrison, a Quaker from Baltimore, Maryland, burned what he said was himself. You, Robert McNamara, burned what you said was a concentration of the Enemy Aggressor. No news medium troubled to place it in quotation marks.

And Norman Morrison, a Quaker from Baltimore, Maryland, burned what he said was himself. He said it with simple materials, such as might be found in your kitchen. In your office, you were informed. Reporters frantically set to work pursuing the angle of mental disturbance. So far, nothing has turned up.

Norman Morrison, a Quaker from Baltimore, Maryland, burned, and while burning, screamed. No warning. No release. Nothing to quote, nothing to manage to place in quotation marks. Pity the unaccustomed hesitance of the newspaper editorialists. Pity the press photographers, who were not called.

Norman Morrison, a Quaker from Baltimore, Maryland, burned and was burned, and said all that there is to say in that language—twice what is said in yours. It is a strange sect, Mr. McNamara, counseled to attempt the whole of a thought in silence, and to oneself.
outputs.L2:
Stephen Smith, a sophomore at the University of Iowa, set fire to what he identified as his draft card; Norman Morrison, a Quaker from Baltimore, Maryland, set fire to what he identified as his own body. You, Robert McNamara, set fire to what you described as a massing of the enemy aggressor. The news outlets did not bother to place that phrase inside quotation marks.

And Norman Morrison, the Baltimore Quaker, burned what he said was himself. He made his statement with plain materials, the sort that might be found in an ordinary kitchen. Word reached you in your office. Journalists immediately hurried to explain it as possible mental instability. As yet, no evidence has appeared.

Norman Morrison, Quaker, Baltimore, Maryland, burned, and as he burned, he cried out. There had been no advance notice, no prepared statement, no press release—nothing convenient for reporters to cite between quotation marks. Spare a thought for the editorial writers, unused to such uncertainty. Spare one, too, for the photographers, who had not been summoned.

Norman Morrison, the Quaker from Baltimore, burned, was consumed, and in that act expressed everything that could be expressed in that language—twice as much as is expressed in yours. It is an unusual faith, Mr. McNamara, one that counsels a person to test an entire thought in silence, within the self.

Stephen Smith reportedly burned his draft card as a protest against the Vietnam War, but Norman Morrison carried protest to a far more extreme and shocking level: he burned himself. Morrison’s self-immolation is presented not simply as an act of despair, but as a deliberate moral gesture against the violence of the war.

The passage contrasts Morrison’s action with the role of Robert McNamara, then Secretary of Defense, who was associated with the bombing and destruction of what official language described as “a concentration of the Enemy Aggressor.” This contrast is central: Morrison destroyed his own body in protest, while McNamara represented a government machine responsible for destroying others through war. The official phrase “Enemy Aggressor” suggests the cold, impersonal language used to justify violence, while Morrison’s act exposed the human cost behind such words.

The media, faced with Morrison’s dramatic and disturbing protest, tried to interpret it through familiar explanations. Reporters considered whether his self-immolation might have been the result of mental instability or emotional disturbance. However, they found no evidence to support that interpretation. Morrison’s act could not easily be dismissed as madness, which made it even more unsettling. It appeared to be a conscious and purposeful act of witness.

Unlike many public protests, Morrison’s self-immolation was not staged for attention. He left no prepared statement for journalists, arranged no photographers, and made no effort to publicize himself. There were no slogans, speeches, or interviews for the press to quote. His silence made the act harder to contain within ordinary media narratives.

The passage suggests that this silence gave Morrison’s protest its power. In contrast to the official language of war—abstract, bureaucratic, and dehumanizing—Morrison’s act communicated directly and painfully. Without words, he forced attention onto the moral horror of violence itself. His protest implied that the reality of war could not be fully expressed through government phrases or newspaper explanations; instead, his burning body became a terrible and unforgettable statement.
outputs.L4:
The text presents a forceful condemnation of the Vietnam War and of the language used by officials and the media to disguise its violence. At its center is the contrast between Norman Morrison, who burned himself to death in protest outside the Pentagon, and Robert McNamara, the Secretary of Defense whose public statements reduced the destruction of war to cold, technical phrases. By placing these two figures side by side, the text exposes the gap between lived moral horror and bureaucratic explanation.

Morrison’s act is shown as a desperate but deeply meaningful form of witness. He does not argue, justify, or explain himself through political language. Instead, his body becomes the statement. His silence is presented as more honest than the speeches and press releases that surround the war, because it refuses to soften or conceal the reality of suffering. In his self-immolation, Morrison makes visible the human cost that official language tries to hide.

By contrast, McNamara’s language represents the machinery of government and military power. Words that might sound neutral or strategic—terms describing bombing, destruction, targets, losses, and military operations—are exposed as euphemisms. They turn death into policy, suffering into calculation, and devastation into administrative procedure. The text criticizes this kind of language because it allows leaders and citizens to discuss mass violence without fully confronting its moral meaning.

The media, too, is implicated in this criticism. Journalistic framing often repeats or legitimizes official vocabulary, helping to normalize war by presenting it in detached, impersonal terms. Instead of naming violence directly, reports may rely on phrases that make destruction seem routine, necessary, or abstract. In doing so, the media can become part of the same system of concealment, translating human agony into acceptable public discourse.

The text therefore argues that Morrison’s protest cuts through this false language. His death cannot easily be absorbed into the familiar vocabulary of strategy and policy. It interrupts the smooth surface of official explanation and forces attention back to the moral reality of the war. His action suggests that when public language becomes corrupted—when it no longer tells the truth about suffering—truth may have to appear in another form.

Ultimately, the text condemns not only the Vietnam War itself but also the ways in which language can be used to make war seem rational, distant, and clean. Morrison’s silent sacrifice is portrayed as more truthful than the statements of powerful officials because it confronts violence directly. Against the empty abstractions of bureaucracy and journalism, his bodily protest reveals the war’s cruelty and the moral failure of those who tried to describe it without truly naming it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short prose-poem in the style of 1960s antiwar literature addressing Robert McNamara after Norman Morrison’s self-immolation.
counterfactuals.output:
Mr. McNamara, outside your window a man became a question made of fire.

He did not bring a rifle, nor a flag, nor a speech polished for the evening news. He brought his body, the last poor match left to the citizen, and struck it against the marble of your war. In his arms, the rumor of children. In the air, the old American hymn turning to smoke.

What did the numbers say then? Did the graphs lean closer? Did the villages, counted in briefings and erased by weather reports, rise for a moment in the glass? A human being burned where policy could see him.

We are told this is not the way to speak. We are told to write letters, to wait, to trust the men with maps. But the maps are red at the edges, and the letters come back folded around silence.

Mr. McNamara, he has entered your ledger now: one flame in Washington answering many flames in Vietnam. Do not call it madness before you have named the madness that required it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a satirical news-report-style monologue contrasting media treatment of draft card burning with Norman Morrison’s protest against the Vietnam War.
counterfactuals.output:
Good evening. Tonight’s top story: America continues its careful, principled debate over the most shocking form of antiwar protest known to civilized society — the burning of small rectangular pieces of paper.

Yes, draft card burning has once again ignited national outrage, proving that while war may be complicated, symbols are refreshingly flammable. Across the country, commentators are asking the hard questions: What happens when a young man destroys a government document? Does democracy survive? Can civilization endure the sight of cardstock curling at the edges?

Congress, never one to be distracted by minor overseas matters such as villages, napalm, or body counts, has moved swiftly to defend the dignity of paperwork. Officials assure the public that the real tragedy of Vietnam is not necessarily the war itself, but the possibility that someone might express opposition to it in a way that makes the evening news uncomfortable.

Meanwhile, in a quieter corner of the national conscience, we remember Norman Morrison, the Quaker pacifist who in 1965 set himself on fire outside the Pentagon to protest the war in Vietnam. His act was not symbolic in the tidy, prosecutable sense. It did not involve a card, a slogan, or a campus rally. It involved a human being turning his own body into an accusation.

Naturally, this presented a problem for the media.

A burned draft card could be debated. It could be photographed, denounced, clipped into a segment, and filed under “youth unrest.” It was dramatic but manageable — a neat little flame in the national living room.

Morrison’s protest was different. It resisted conversion into a panel discussion. It asked too much. It did not merely challenge policy; it challenged the viewer. It suggested that perhaps the violence worth condemning was not only the visible fire of protest, but the distant fire delivered in America’s name.

And so the machinery of interpretation got to work. Draft card burners were radicals, lawbreakers, provocateurs. Morrison was tragic, disturbed, perhaps too sincere to be politically useful. The former could be made into a controversy. The latter had to be made into an anomaly.

Because if a man burns a card, the question is: “Should he be punished?”

But if a man burns himself outside the Pentagon, the question becomes: “What kind of war makes someone believe this is the only language left?”

And that question, viewers, is much harder to fit between commercial breaks.

So tonight we return to our regularly scheduled programming: solemn concern for order, reverence for documents, and restrained discomfort with anyone who insists that moral horror should interrupt the broadcast. Stay tuned for our next segment: “Patriotism and Proper Fire Safety — Why Some Flames Offend Us More Than Others.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a literary passage about Norman Morrison, the Quaker who burned himself outside the Pentagon, using repetition and irony to criticize McNamara and the press.
counterfactuals.output:
Norman Morrison came to the Pentagon carrying no weapon, and so the armed building did not know what to do with him.

He came with the quiet of a meetinghouse still clinging to his coat, with the plain, impossible vocabulary of the Friends: peace, conscience, witness. He came to the place where numbers were washed and dressed for dinner—sorties, tonnage, targets, collateral—where the dead were made presentable by arithmetic. He came to the river of corridors and the polished rooms, to the nation’s great counting-house of fire, and he answered fire with fire.

And Robert McNamara looked down, or did not look down. He saw, or did not see. He knew, or did not know. This was the genius of power: to be always informed and always innocent, always briefed and always surprised. On his desk the war arrived in folders, clipped and typed, casualty estimates in disciplined columns. Outside his window a man became an estimate that would not stay in its column.

The secretaries ran. The guards ran. The flames rose.

The press came too, faithful as rain after thunder. They asked the necessary questions, which is to say the smallest ones. How old was he? Where was he from? Was he disturbed? Was he alone? Had he left a note? They examined the match and not the pyre, the gesture and not the war, the body and not the bodies. A Quaker had burned himself before the temple of policy, and the headline went searching for a diagnosis.

A troubled man, they wrote.

Troubled, yes. Troubled by children burning in villages whose names the presses misspelled. Troubled by the efficient sorrow of men who could say “regrettable” without regret. Troubled by napalm, troubled by briefings, troubled by the clean hands of those who ordered dirty weather over distant fields. Troubled, as water is troubled by a stone dropped into it. Troubled, as a bell is troubled into ringing.

McNamara had numbers. Morrison had a body.

McNamara had charts. Morrison had silence.

McNamara had the grave courtesy of committees, the mild voice that could make apocalypse sound managerial. Morrison had the terrible eloquence of no longer arguing. There is an irony there, if irony is still permitted among the ruins: the man of peace chose flame, and the men of war chose language; the one who burned was called irrational, and the ones who burned villages were called responsible.

The Pentagon endured, of course. Buildings are excellent survivors. They are made for weather, for history, for the inconveniences of conscience. The next morning the doors opened. The papers folded. The elevators rose. The war continued its professional breathing.

But somewhere in the official air, something would not be filed.

Norman Morrison stood outside the machinery and made himself a question it could not answer. Not because fire is holy. Not because death is persuasive. Not because despair should be imitated. But because a nation had grown fluent in distance, and he abolished distance. He brought the burning back to the burners. He placed, for one unbearable moment, the war at the doorstep of the war-makers.

And the press said: spectacle.

And the office said: tragedy.

And the conscience said: witness.

Again and again, the words returned, stripped of their uniforms: What did you see? What did you know? What did you do?

McNamara had numbers. Morrison had a name.

And the name would not burn away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: In a poetic, accusatory voice, address Robert McNamara directly and compare official language about bombing Vietnam to the silent protest of a Quaker pacifist.
counterfactuals.output:
Robert McNamara,  
you polished the nouns until they no longer bled.

You called it *attrition*,  
as if grief were a column of figures,  
as if fire could be filed under policy,  
as if a village, once lifted into smoke,  
became only a problem of metrics.

Your language wore a suit.  
It stood at the podium with clean hands.  
It said *targets*, *sorties*, *pacification*,  
said *collateral* where a mother had been,  
said *pressure* where the sky opened  
and poured metal on the rice fields.

And against all that machinery of speech  
stood the Quaker pacifist—silent,  
hat in hand, eyes lowered not in shame  
but in refusal.

No charts.  
No euphemisms.  
No arithmetic of acceptable sorrow.

Only the plain testimony of a body  
unwilling to bless the bomb,  
a stillness louder than your briefings,  
a silence that accused every syllable  
you sent out to soften the sound of burning.

You measured death, Robert,  
but he would not measure peace.  
You named destruction with official care,  
but he answered with the terrible clarity  
of saying nothing—  
and making your words sound like ash.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an anti-Vietnam War prose poem with repeated references to “Norman Morrison, Quaker, of Baltimore Maryland,” emphasizing silence, quotation marks, and media hypocrisy.
counterfactuals.output:
“Norman Morrison, Quaker, of Baltimore Maryland,” they said, and then the microphones lowered their silver heads.

Silence entered the broadcast booth like smoke.

“Norman Morrison, Quaker, of Baltimore Maryland,” stood in the place where the official language failed—where “pacification” meant fire, where “targets” meant children, where “necessary escalation” meant the sky learning to burn.

The newspapers put quotation marks around grief.  
They put quotation marks around witness.  
They put quotation marks around “peace,” as if peace were a rumor, as if mercy needed verification from a Pentagon clerk.

And the war went on speaking fluently in numbers.

“Norman Morrison, Quaker, of Baltimore Maryland,” became a sentence nobody wanted to finish. A man with a name, a faith, a city, a family—reduced by evening panels to “an incident,” “a disturbance,” “a tragic gesture,” words chosen for their clean cuffs and bloodless shoes.

Silence.

Not the silence of absence, but the silence after a door has been opened and no one dares look inside. The silence of editors deciding column inches. The silence of men in suits saying “regrettable” while maps glowed behind them. The silence of a country learning to place quotation marks around its conscience.

“Norman Morrison, Quaker, of Baltimore Maryland,” they repeated, but not enough to hear him.

They showed the war in fragments: a helmet, a hill, a briefing, a flag. They did not show the grammar of napalm. They did not translate the screams. They did not ask why the word “security” always seemed to require someone else’s village.

They asked whether his act was “sane.”  
They did not ask whether the war was sane.  
They asked whether protest had gone “too far.”  
They did not ask how far a bomb falls.

“Norman Morrison, Quaker, of Baltimore Maryland,” was framed as spectacle by those who sold spectacle nightly between advertisements for soap, cars, and cigarettes—clean hands, open roads, smooth breathing—while across the ocean, the air itself became an enemy.

Silence again.

A Quaker silence, perhaps: waiting, inward, severe. A silence that refuses applause. A silence that indicts. A silence standing barefoot before the machinery of explanation.

And still the cameras blinked.

They loved quotation marks: “collateral,” “containment,” “credibility,” “victory.” Little fences around enormous lies. Little hooks from which to hang the dead until they no longer looked like the dead.

“Norman Morrison, Quaker, of Baltimore Maryland,” did not fit the script. He was not a statistic, not a slogan, not a cleanly edited debate. He was a question burning at the edge of empire’s desk.

What kind of nation needs so many euphemisms?

What kind of screen can show fire and call it policy?

What kind of silence follows the truth?

“Norman Morrison, Quaker, of Baltimore Maryland,” said nothing that could be clipped into a favorable sound bite. His silence was the refusal of quotation marks. His silence was not “balanced.” His silence did not invite the other side of burning children.

The anchors adjusted their voices.  
The officials adjusted their statements.  
The war adjusted its aim.

But somewhere beyond the studio lights, beyond the print deadline, beyond the careful phrases and patriotic music, a name remained:

“Norman Morrison, Quaker, of Baltimore Maryland.”

And around that name, silence.

Not emptiness.

Judgment.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
